To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Bayesian approach to active learning is an excellent framework for modeling adaptive information filtering and that the Bayesian framework is well-suited for exploring the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation in active learning

(1) Bayesian active learning can be successfully applied to the task of adaptive filtering; (2) Bayesian active learning is more effective than traditional adaptive filtering in terms of both accuracy and efficiency; (3) Bayesian active learning outperforms traditional adaptive filtering in the case where there is no prior knowledge about the user, as well as when the system has a prior knowledge of the user; (4) The performance of Bayesian active learning is not significantly affected by the size of the prior knowledge;
the Bayesian active learning approach is a promising direction for adaptive information filtering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: "How can an agent learn to explore its environment to find new opportunities and then exploit those opportunities to maximize its reward?"

the following questions: How can we design an adaptive filtering system that is aware of and takes advantage of the two effects of filtering? How can we model the user's changing information needs? How can we learn from the user's feedback in a way that is consistent with the model of changing information needs?
how to improve the performance of adaptive information filtering by exploiting the user feedback in an optimal way.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Bayesian approach is the best choice for adaptive filtering, as it provides a framework for modeling both the user's information seeking behavior as well as the system's learning behavior.
the Bayesian Active Learning approach is the most efficient way of learning the user profile.

the traditional approach to adaptive filtering does not model the fact that a document can satisfy the user in two ways: by delivering the document immediately, and by improving the model of the user.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are developing a Bayesian framework that can learn the user's information interests from relevance feedback, and then use this knowledge to filter future documents.
we propose to use Bayesian Active Learning to model the second effect and to use this model to guide filtering.
we have shown how Bayesian active learning can be used in an adaptive information filtering setting to model both effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a system should not only filter the stream of documents but also explore the user's information landscape to find out what information needs to be filtered in the first place.
the traditional approach to adaptive filtering is not optimal, and that it can be improved by using the principles of exploration and exploitation from reinforcement learning.
it is important to model both effects in adaptive filtering and that this can be accomplished by applying Bayesian active learning to the task.
